definition: Bradford's law is a pattern first described by Samuel C.
details: Bradford in 1934 that estimates the exponentially diminishing returns of searching for references in science journals. One formulation is that if journals in a field are sorted by number of articles into three groups, each with about one-third of all articles, then the number of journals in each group will be proportional to 1:n:n2. There are a number of related formulations of the principle. In many disciplines, this pattern is called a Pareto distribution. As a practical example, suppose that a researcher has five core scientific journals for his or her subject. Suppose that in a month there are 12 articles of interest in those journals. Suppose further that in order to find another dozen articles of interest, the researcher would have to go to an additional 10 journals. Then that researcher's Bradford multiplier bm is 2 (i.e. 10/5). For each new dozen articles, that researcher will need to look in bm times as many journals. After looking in 5, 10, 20, 40, etc. journals, most researchers quickly realize that there is little point in looking further. Different researchers have different numbers of core journals, and different Bradford multipliers. But the pattern holds quite well across many subjects, and may well be a general pattern for human interactions in social systems. Like Zipf's law, to which it is related, we do not have a good explanation for why it works, but knowing that it does is very useful for librarians. What it means is that for each specialty, it is sufficient to identify the "core publications" for that field and only stock those; very rarely will researchers need to go outside that set. However, its impact has been far greater than that. Armed with this idea and inspired by Vannevar Bush's famous article As We May Think, Eugene Garfield at the Institute for Scientific Information in the 1960s developed a comprehensive index of how scientific thinking propagates. His Science Citation Index (SCI) made it easy to identify exactly which scientists did science that had an impact, and which journals that science appeared in. It also caused the discovery, which some did not expect, that a few journals, such as Nature and Science, were core for all of hard science. The same pattern does not happen with the humanities or the social sciences. The result of this is pressure on scientists to publish in the best journals, and pressure on universities to ensure access to that core set of journals. On the other hand, the set of "core journals" may vary more or less strongly with individual researchers, and even more strongly along schools-of-thought divides. There is also a danger of over-representing majority views if journals are selected in this fashion.

explainer.lead: Bradford's law describes a common pattern in scientific publishing: a small set of journals supplies many relevant articles, while finding more articles requires searching rapidly growing numbers of journals. It helps librarians focus on a field's core publications and helps explain why those journals can become so influential.

tiers.eli5: Imagine looking for your favorite songs: a few playlists contain most of them, but finding each new batch means checking more and more playlists. Bradford's law says scientific articles often behave the same way. Librarians can use that pattern to choose the most useful journals without expecting them to contain everything.
tiers.practitioner: Use it when prioritizing journal collections or scoping a literature search: identify a specialty's core publications, then expect sharply diminishing returns as the search expands. The number of core journals and the multiplier vary by researcher and subject, so do not treat a fixed journal set as complete. Selecting only majority-view journals can also over-represent dominant schools of thought.
tiers.paperLevel: One formulation sorts journals by article count and divides the articles into three roughly equal groups; the journal counts in those groups are proportional to 1:n:n². Samuel C. Bradford first described the pattern in 1934, and related formulations exist, including descriptions as a Pareto distribution in many disciplines. The pattern fits many subjects but lacks a good explanation, core sets can vary across researchers and schools of thought, and the same pattern does not occur in the humanities or social sciences.

explainer.example: A researcher finds 12 articles of interest in five core journals. Finding another 12 requires 10 additional journals, giving a Bradford multiplier of 10/5 = 2. Each further dozen articles therefore requires twice as many journals, following the progression 5, 10, 20, 40, until searching further offers little value.

usedIn.name: Library collection management
usedIn.detail: Librarians identify and stock a specialty's core journals because researchers rarely need to search beyond them.

usedIn.name: Science Citation Index
usedIn.detail: Eugene Garfield's index built on the idea to trace scientific influence and identify impactful scientists and journals.

usedIn.name: Scientific publishing
usedIn.detail: The concentration of important work in a few journals contributes to pressure to publish in leading journals and to provide access to them.

explainer.intuition: Relevant articles are unevenly spread across journals. The first useful articles come from a compact core, but each additional batch demands a much wider search, so effort grows faster than the return.
howItWorks: Sort a field's journals by how many relevant articles they contain.
Group the journals so each group accounts for about one-third of all articles.
Compare group sizes: their journal counts are proportional to 1:n:n².
Use the multiplier to estimate how much wider each further search must become.
Stop expanding when the extra articles no longer justify the additional journals.
explainer.whyItMatters: It gives librarians a practical basis for concentrating collections on core publications. Its influence also reached citation analysis through Garfield's Science Citation Index, which revealed that journals such as Nature and Science were core across the hard sciences.
misconceptions: It is not a guarantee that core journals contain every article a researcher needs.
There is no single core set or multiplier shared by every researcher and school of thought.
The pattern is not equally applicable everywhere; it does not occur the same way in the humanities or social sciences.
